analysis.one_liner: Redirects every asbestos injury claim through a new federal medical-screening agency before victims may sue.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after one subcommittee hearing in October 1999, it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the 106th Congress ended, despite 29 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an 'Asbestos Resolution Corporation' that every asbestos claimant would have to pass through before setting foot in court. A worker would first need a certificate of medical eligibility under strict federal criteria, then go through mandatory mediation and possibly arbitration before being allowed to file any lawsuit. It would bar class actions unless every defendant agrees, apply retroactively to cases already pending, and charge defendant companies for the new system's costs. Sponsors said this would fix a slow, expensive litigation mess; its practical effect would be to sharply cut the number of sick workers who could recover and the amounts they could win.
analysis.who_benefits: Asbestos defendant companies and their insurers gain the most: claims would be screened out by strict medical criteria, steered into arbitration instead of jury trials, and brought one at a time with no class actions. Some seriously ill claimants also gain — the bill abolishes time-limit defenses, lets workers wait until cancer appears, and makes the government's medical certificate presumptively correct.

how_it_helps.text: The bill abolishes statutes-of-limitation and other timeliness defenses, so a shipyard worker exposed decades ago could still bring a claim, and could wait to see whether an asbestos-related cancer develops rather than being forced to sue early and give up future claims [S2] [S3].

Once the Corporation issues a certificate of medical eligibility, that certificate is presumed correct unless the defendant rebuts it with clear and convincing evidence, which lowers the claimant's burden in arbitration or court [S3].

Claimants are expressly told they are not required to hire a lawyer to file and pursue a claim, and the process promises resolution within set time limits — mediation must conclude within 60 days of the mediator's appointment [S3].

Sponsors argued the current system is broken: their findings state that more than 150,000 asbestos suits are pending, over 15 companies have gone bankrupt, and less than half of litigation costs actually reach claimants [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Asbestos victims whose conditions don't meet the bill's strict medical screens would be locked out of compensation entirely. Even claimants who qualify would lose the right to a jury trial until after mandatory mediation, could not join together in class actions without each defendant's consent, and could not recover punitive damages through collective proceedings. The rules would apply retroactively to cases already in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick asbestos workers and their families

drawbacks.text: The medical criteria are strict cutoffs, not just screening. Asbestosis claims require specified lung-function thresholds, and lung cancer claimants can count years of exposure only before 1979 (with narrow exceptions) toward a 15-year exposure requirement — a worker exposed mainly after 1979 could fail to qualify no matter how sick [S3].

No civil asbestos lawsuit could be filed or maintained without a certificate of medical eligibility and a release from mediation, and no class action or consolidation would be allowed without the consent of every defendant — eliminating the collective tools plaintiffs used against dozens of defendants at once [S2] [S3].
The Act would apply to any pending asbestos case that has not reached a final, nonappealable judgment, overriding the rules those suits were filed under [S2] [S3].

Claimants denied under the standard criteria could only reach an 'exceptional medical claims' panel by proving, with clear and convincing evidence, that their condition is substantially comparable to a qualifying one — a very high bar for people already seriously ill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targeted was real: asbestos litigation was slow, expensive, and unpredictable, and the sponsors' own findings concede that less than half the money spent ever reached sick people [S3]. But the remedy was written largely around defendants' interests. Rigid exposure cutoffs, mandatory mediation, a ban on class actions without unanimous defendant consent, and retroactive application would have kept many genuinely sick workers out of court and shrunk recoveries for those who got in, while the companies footing the bill for the new system would be the same companies whose liability it reduces. A narrower fix that preserved jury access for the seriously ill might have helped both sides; this version would not.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in October 1999, and was never reported out or voted on before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. John Ashcroft introduced the bill on March 25, 1999, joined by eight original cosponsors including Judiciary Chairman Orrin Hatch and Democrats Christopher Dodd, Joseph Lieberman, and Charles Schumer [S3] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, which never reported it to the full Senate [S5].
The Judiciary Subcommittee on Administrative Oversight and the Courts held hearings on October 5, 1999 [S5].
Ashcroft made further introductory remarks on April 4, 2000, but no committee or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The bill attracted 29 cosponsors — 24 Republicans and 5 Democrats — but the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still stalled in committee [S1] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, asbestos victims and their families kept full access to the courts, and defendant companies remained exposed to jury trials, class actions, and the full damages rules in state law. Plaintiffs' asbestos attorneys kept the case flow the bill would have restricted; defendants gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: 29 cosponsors split 24 Republicans and 5 Democrats, and the original group ranged from conservatives (Hatch, Grassley, Sessions) to liberals (Dodd, Lieberman, Schumer). No floor vote ever occurred to test the split.

industries.industry: Asbestos product manufacturers and other defendant companies
industries.note: The bill would screen out many claimants with strict medical criteria, force the rest into mediation and arbitration rather than jury trials, bar class actions without each defendant's consent, and apply retroactively to pending suits — all of which shrink the liability that had already driven more than 15 asbestos companies into bankruptcy [S2] [S3]. Sick workers would bear the cost in excluded claims and smaller, slower recoveries [S3].

Capping and channeling asbestos liability into a predictable, defendant-funded administrative process reduces the open-ended court judgments and settlements insurers stand behind [S3]. The savings come out of what victims could recover [S2] [S3].

Mandatory medical certification, required mediation, per-claim individual proceedings with no class actions, and restrictions on attorney fee awards would sharply cut both the volume of filings and the fees available to lawyers representing asbestos victims [S2] [S3].

The bill exempts trusts already operating from court-supervised asbestos bankruptcy plans, unless they choose to opt in, leaving those trusts as the standing channel for claims against bankrupt companies [S3].
